title: Quiz 3: Supervised and Unsupervised Learning, and Neural Networks
description: 198 questions on supervised learning, evaluation metrics, cross-validation, KNN, decision trees, random forests, regression, clustering, PCA and neural networks, with short-answer practice. Choose which topics and how many questions.

questions.question: A hospital holds 5,000 past patient records, each with lab values and a note of whether the patient was readmitted within 30 days. Which kind of learning does this data suit?
options: Unsupervised learning, because the lab values are numbers that can be grouped by similarity
Supervised learning, because every record carries the known outcome to learn from
Dimensionality reduction, because the many lab values can be merged into a few new columns
Clustering, because patients with similar records can be placed in the same group
questions.explanation: A recorded outcome for every row is a label, which is what supervised learning needs.

questions.question: Which prediction task is a regression problem?
options: Deciding whether a used car will pass or fail its yearly inspection
Sorting used cars into economy, family or luxury categories by features
Estimating the selling price of a used car from its age and mileage
Flagging used car listings as genuine or fraudulent from their details
questions.explanation: Regression predicts a number on a continuous scale. The others each predict a category.

questions.question: A model must label each support ticket as one of five product categories. What kind of task is this?
options: Regression: the target is a number that can fall anywhere on a scale
Clustering: the target groups are discovered from the data itself
Regression: the five categories are coded as the numbers 1 to 5
Classification: the target is one of a fixed set of categories
questions.explanation: Coding categories as numbers does not make the target continuous. A fixed set of labels is classification.

questions.question: A table is built to predict whether a customer will cancel a subscription. Which column is the target?
options: The column recording whether each past customer did cancel
The column holding each customer's monthly bill amount
The column listing each customer's unique ID number
The column counting each customer's support calls this year
questions.explanation: The target is the answer the model learns to predict. The other columns are candidate features (or an ID that carries no information).

questions.question: Why is accuracy measured on a test set instead of on the rows the model trained on?
options: Training rows are always too few to give a score that means anything
Rows it already saw can be memorized, so they do not show how it handles new data
Scores on training rows cannot be computed once the model has finished fitting
Test rows are cleaner than training rows because they were checked for errors
questions.explanation: The aim is to estimate performance on unseen data. A model can score well on rows it memorized and still fail on new ones.

questions.question: A labeled dataset of 600 rows is split with test_size=0.25. How many rows are used for training?
options: 150 rows
300 rows
450 rows
475 rows
questions.explanation: The test set is 600 x 0.25 = 150 rows, leaving 600 - 150 = 450 to train on.

questions.question: Which order of steps is correct for a supervised learning workflow?
options: Fit on all the data, split it afterwards, predict on the training part, compare with the known labels
Split the data, fit on the test part, predict on the training part, compare with the new labels
Predict on the test part, fit on the training part, split the data, compare with the known labels
Split the data, fit on the training part, predict on the test part, compare with the known labels
questions.explanation: The model must learn from training rows only, then be judged on test rows whose answers it has not seen.

questions.question: In scikit-learn, what does model.predict(x_test) return?
options: The model's predicted target for every row of x_test
The true target values for every row of x_test
The accuracy score of the model on x_test
A new set of features computed from x_test
questions.explanation: predict returns predictions. They are then compared with y_test, the true answers.

questions.question: A classification model's target is a number that can take any value on a continuous scale.
questions.explanation: That describes a regression target. A classification target is a category.

questions.question: In supervised learning, the training data must include the correct answer for every row.
questions.explanation: Those correct answers are the labels the model learns the mapping from.

questions.question: Match each task to the kind of problem it is.

pairs.right: Regression

pairs.left: Decide whether a photo shows a cat or a dog
pairs.right: Classification

pairs.left: Group news articles by theme with no labels
pairs.right: Clustering
Dimensionality reduction

questions.question: A supervised problem whose target is a category is called ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Classification predicts categories; regression predicts numbers.

questions.question: A spam filter flags 50 emails and 40 of them really are spam. What is its precision, and what does that measure?
options: 0.80: of all the spam that arrived, 80% was caught by the filter
0.80: of the emails flagged as spam, 80% really were spam
0.20: of the emails flagged as spam, 20% really were spam
0.40: of all the emails in the inbox, 40% were flagged as spam
questions.explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50. It looks only at the rows the model flagged positive.

questions.question: A screening test finds 45 of the 60 people who actually have a condition. What is its recall?
options: 0.25 (the 15 missed out of 60)
questions.explanation: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 45 / 60 = 0.75.

questions.question: A fraud model scans card purchases. Which outcome is a false positive?
options: A fraudulent purchase that the model lets through as genuine
A fraudulent purchase that the model correctly blocks as fraud
A genuine purchase that the model correctly approves as genuine
A genuine purchase that the model blocks as fraud
questions.explanation: A false positive is a wrong 'positive' call, where positive means fraud here. Letting fraud through is a false negative.

questions.question: A line has 990 normal parts and 10 defective ones. A model labels all 1,000 as normal. Which statement is true?
options: Accuracy is 99%, but recall for defective parts is 0, so it is useless for finding defects
Accuracy is 99% and recall for defective parts is 99%, so it finds nearly all defects
Accuracy is 50% and recall for defective parts is 0, since it guessed a single class
Accuracy is 1% and recall for defective parts is 100%, since it ignored normal parts
questions.explanation: 990 of 1,000 are right (99%), but not one defect is found. Accuracy hides this when classes are imbalanced.

questions.question: For which job is high recall the main priority?
options: Cleaning a newsletter list, where wrongly removing a subscriber is the worst outcome
Screening luggage for dangerous items, where a missed item is the worst outcome
Recommending films, where showing a poor suggestion is the worst outcome
Flagging plagiarism for penalties, where accusing an honest student is the worst outcome
questions.explanation: Recall counts how many real positives are found, so it matters most when a miss (false negative) is costly. The others are costly false positives, which precision tracks.

questions.question: What does the F1-score combine?
options: Accuracy and recall, in an arithmetic mean that stays high if either one is high
Precision and accuracy, in a product that grows as the number of classes grows
Precision and recall, in a harmonic mean that stays low if either one is low
True positives and true negatives, in a ratio that shrinks as the dataset grows
questions.explanation: F1 = 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall). It rewards a balance of the two.

questions.question: A model has precision 0.60 and recall 0.30. What is its F1-score?
questions.explanation: F1 = 2 x 0.60 x 0.30 / (0.60 + 0.30) = 0.36 / 0.90 = 0.40. The simple average (0.45) would overstate it.

questions.question: What does mean squared error (MSE) measure for a regression model?
options: The average of the squared gaps between actual and predicted values
The share of the target's variation that the model accounts for
The average of the signed gaps between actual and predicted values, so errors cancel
The count of predictions that landed exactly on the actual value
questions.explanation: Squaring stops positive and negative errors cancelling and punishes large misses. The share of variation explained is R-squared.

questions.question: A regression model's R-squared on held-out data comes out negative, at -0.4. How should that be read?
options: It explains 40% of the variance, with the minus sign showing the direction
It predicts worse than always guessing the mean of the target
It has a mean squared error of 0.4, which means it fits the data well
The model is broken, because R-squared cannot go below zero
questions.explanation: R-squared 0 equals predicting the mean. On unseen data it can fall below 0 for a model that is worse than that.

questions.question: Which pair of metrics is used to judge a regression model?
options: Precision and recall
Accuracy and F1-score
Mean squared error and R-squared
Sensitivity and a confusion matrix
questions.explanation: MSE and R-squared score numeric predictions. The others score classifiers.

questions.question: On a test set, a classifier has TP 35, FP 5, FN 15 and TN 45. What is its accuracy?
questions.explanation: Correct = 35 + 45 = 80 out of 100 rows. 0.70 is recall (35 / 50) and 0.875 is precision (35 / 40).

questions.question: A model can have high accuracy and still be poor at finding the minority class.
questions.explanation: With imbalanced classes the majority class dominates the accuracy figure.

questions.question: Recall is calculated as TP / (TP + FP).
questions.explanation: That is precision. Recall is TP / (TP + FN).

questions.question: Match each metric to the question it answers.

pairs.right: What share of all predictions were correct?
Of the rows flagged positive, how many really were?
Of the rows that really were positive, how many were found?
How balanced are precision and recall?

questions.question: The metric TP / (TP + FN), the share of real positives that are found, is called ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Recall, also called sensitivity or the true positive rate.

questions.question: A model reaches 99% on its training rows and 71% on its test rows. How should this be described?
options: Overfitting: it memorized details of the training rows that do not carry over
Underfitting: it is too simple to capture the pattern in either set of rows
Good generalization: scoring higher on training rows is expected and harmless
Data leakage: the test rows were accidentally included in the training data
questions.explanation: A large drop from training to test is the sign of overfitting. Leakage would inflate the test score instead.

questions.question: A straight-line model scores 58% on training rows and 57% on test rows, though the true pattern is clearly curved. What is the likely cause?
options: Overfitting: the model has memorized noise in the training rows
Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the curve
High variance: the model changes a lot between training samples
Class imbalance: the model has ignored the minority class
questions.explanation: Low scores on both sets point to underfitting, which is high bias.

questions.question: In 10-fold cross-validation on 500 rows, how many rows are in each validation fold and how many models are trained?
options: 50 rows per fold; 1 model
10 rows per fold; 50 models
50 rows per fold; 10 models
450 rows per fold; 10 models
questions.explanation: 500 / 10 = 50 rows per fold, and one model is trained for each fold, validating on that fold and training on the other nine.

questions.question: When is stratified k-fold preferred over plain k-fold?
options: When the target is a number, so each fold needs to keep the same average
When the rows are in time order, so each fold needs to keep that order
When the dataset is tiny, so each fold needs to hold exactly one row
When one class is rare, so each fold needs to keep the same class proportions
questions.explanation: Stratification keeps the class mix of the full data in every fold, which matters when a class is rare.

questions.question: What is leave-one-out cross-validation?
options: k-fold where k equals the number of rows, so each row is validated once on its own
k-fold where k equals 2, so the data is split into halves that swap roles
A single split that leaves one feature out of the model each time
A method that removes one outlier row before each training run
questions.explanation: It trains one model per row, which is thorough but expensive, so it is used on small datasets.

questions.question: Two years of daily sales are used to predict future sales. Which validation is appropriate?
options: Shuffle all days randomly and use plain k-fold so each fold is varied
Train on earlier days and validate on later days, never shuffling the order
Validate on the earliest days and train on later days to test the model hard
Use leave-one-out so each day is predicted from days on both sides of it
questions.explanation: A model must not learn from the future to predict the past. Time-ordered data needs a forward-looking split.

questions.question: One model beats another on a single 80/20 split. Why check with cross-validation before choosing it?
options: The single split trains on too few rows for either model to learn anything
Cross-validation always shows that the more complex model is the better one
The win may depend on which rows landed in the test set; folds average that out
A single split cannot produce a usable accuracy score for a model at all
questions.explanation: One split's score can be lucky or unlucky. The average of several folds is a more stable estimate.

questions.question: How is cross-validation used when choosing a hyperparameter such as k in KNN?
options: Train once with each k and keep whichever scored best on the test set
Pick the k that gives the highest training accuracy across all the folds
Choose k at random inside each fold and average the chosen values
Score each candidate k across the folds and keep the k with the best average
questions.explanation: Tuning on the test set would leak it. Cross-validation scores on held-out folds inside the training data.

questions.question: Which change is most likely to reduce overfitting in a deep decision tree?
options: Limit the tree's depth or prune its branches so it cannot memorize rows
Let the tree grow until every leaf holds a single training row
Remove the test set so that all rows are used for learning
Add more splits so the tree fits the training rows more closely
questions.explanation: Constraining complexity (max_depth, pruning) forces the tree to learn general patterns, not individual rows.

questions.question: Which description matches high variance?
options: The fitted model misses the pattern because its assumptions are too simple
The fitted model changes a lot if it is trained on a different sample of the data
The fitted model gives the same predictions no matter which features are used
The fitted model's errors all fall in the same direction as the target
questions.explanation: High variance goes with overfitting. Missing the pattern through simple assumptions is high bias.

questions.question: In k-fold cross-validation, every row is used for validation exactly once.
questions.explanation: Each fold takes one turn as the validation set.

questions.question: A model that scores far higher on its training data than on its test data is underfitting.
questions.explanation: That gap is overfitting. Underfitting scores poorly on both.

questions.question: A model too simple to capture the pattern, scoring poorly on both training and test data, is said to be ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Underfitting means high bias.

questions.question: Match each validation technique to its description.

pairs.right: One single train/test split
Each fold keeps the class proportions
One row validates and all the rest train
Trains on the past and validates on the future

questions.question: A KNN classifier uses k = 3. The three nearest training points to a new row are labeled A, B and A. What class is predicted?
options: B: the neighbor listed second sets the class
A and B: the row receives both labels at once
A: it wins the vote two to one
No class: three neighbors are too few to decide
questions.explanation: KNN takes the majority class among the k nearest neighbors.

questions.question: What is the Euclidean distance between the points (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
questions.explanation: sqrt((4 - 1)^2 + (6 - 2)^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. The value 7 is the Manhattan distance.

questions.question: What is the Manhattan distance between (2, 7) and (6, 4)?
questions.explanation: |6 - 2| + |4 - 7| = 4 + 3 = 7. The value 5 is the Euclidean distance.

questions.question: Which problem is most likely when k is set to 1?
options: Underfitting: the boundary becomes so smooth that it blurs small groups
Overfitting: the boundary follows every point, including noisy ones
Ties: a single neighbor cannot vote, so no class is ever predicted
Slow training: one neighbor needs a model to be built beforehand
questions.explanation: With k = 1 a single mislabeled or noisy point decides its whole neighborhood.

questions.question: k is raised to nearly the size of the whole training set. What happens to the predictions?
options: They match each point's own label, because every vote is decided locally
They become exact, because more neighbors always means more accuracy
They drift toward the majority class, since it dominates nearly every vote
They stop changing between points, because only a single class centroid counts
questions.explanation: A very large k averages over almost everything, so the biggest class wins nearly everywhere: underfitting.

questions.question: What is the soundest way to choose k?
options: Always use the square root of the number of features
Pick the k that gives 100% accuracy on the training rows
Use the largest odd number below the count of rows
Try several values and compare their cross-validated scores
questions.explanation: k is a hyperparameter, so it is tuned on held-out data. k = 1 always scores 100% on training rows, which proves nothing.

questions.question: Which step best prepares features for KNN?
options: Rescale them (min-max or standardization) so each contributes comparably to distances
Sort the rows by the feature with the largest values so close rows sit together
Drop the feature with the smallest values because it adds the least information
Convert every feature to a category so distances are counted in whole steps
questions.explanation: KNN is built on distances, so a feature with huge numbers would swamp the others unless the scales are aligned.

questions.question: At which point does KNN do most of its computing work?
options: During training, when it fits weights to minimize the error on every row
At prediction time, when it measures distances from the new row to the stored rows
During splitting, when it decides which features to rank first
After prediction, when it re-evaluates which stored rows were most useful
questions.explanation: KNN is a lazy learner: training just stores the data.

questions.question: Which is a genuine weakness of KNN?
options: It cannot represent a curved boundary between classes
It needs a long training phase before it can predict anything
Prediction slows as the stored data grows, since every row is compared
It requires the target to be a number rather than a category of any kind
questions.explanation: Each prediction needs distances to all stored rows. KNN makes no straight-line assumption and has no real training phase.

questions.question: How does KNN make a prediction when the target is a number?
options: It takes the most common target value among the k nearest rows
It fits one straight line through the k nearest training rows
It copies the target of the single farthest of the k rows
It averages the target values of the k nearest training rows
questions.explanation: KNN regression averages the neighbors' values. Voting is for classification.

questions.question: Compared with Euclidean distance, Manhattan distance is
options: Measured along the axes, like walking a street grid, with no squaring or square root
Measured as the straight line between the points, using the Pythagorean theorem
Measured on only the feature with the largest gap, ignoring all the other features
Measured as the angle between the two points' feature vectors, ignoring their length
questions.explanation: Manhattan distance sums the gaps along each axis, which is cheaper to compute.

questions.question: KNN needs its features to be scaled for its distances to be meaningful.
questions.explanation: Otherwise the feature with the largest numbers dominates every distance.

questions.question: KNN builds a model during training by fitting a set of weights.
questions.explanation: KNN stores the training data and does its work when a prediction is requested.

questions.question: In KNN, k is a ____ that is set before training rather than learned from the data. (one word)
questions.explanation: Hyperparameters are chosen by the user, often with cross-validation.

questions.question: Explain how KNN classifies a new point, and describe what happens to the decision boundary as k grows from 1 to a large value.
questions.modelAnswer: KNN measures the distance (usually Euclidean, sometimes Manhattan) from the new point to every training point, takes the k closest, and assigns the class that most of them hold. With k = 1 the boundary is jagged and follows every point, including noise, so the model overfits. As k grows the boundary becomes smoother; if k is very large, the majority class dominates and small groups are lost, which is underfitting. Features should be scaled first and k chosen with cross-validation.
rubric: Describes measuring distance to the training points and taking the k nearest
Says the class is chosen by majority vote of those neighbors
Says small k gives a jagged boundary and overfitting
Says large k gives a smooth boundary that leans to the majority class (underfitting)

questions.question: In a fitted decision tree, what does a leaf node hold?
options: A test on one feature that routes rows down a branch
The final prediction for rows that reach it, like a class label
The training row that was nearest to the split point
The feature that was removed because it was found uninformative
questions.explanation: Internal nodes are tests; leaves hold the answer.

questions.question: A node holds 10 rows: 5 of class A and 5 of class B. What is its Gini impurity?
questions.explanation: Gini = 1 - (0.5^2 + 0.5^2) = 0.5, the maximum for two classes.

questions.question: A node holds 10 rows: 9 of class A and 1 of class B. What is its Gini impurity?
What does a Gini impurity of 0 mean for a node?
options: Every row in the node belongs to the same class
The node holds an equal mix of all the classes present
The node has no rows left that could be split further
The node was created by a split that separated nothing
questions.explanation: 0 is a pure node. That is the goal of each split.

questions.question: In a two-class problem, which node has the highest entropy?
options: A node with 90% of its rows in a single class
A node with half its rows in each class
A node where every row is from the same class
A node with 75% of its rows in a single class
questions.explanation: Entropy peaks (1 bit) at an even mix and is 0 for a pure node.

questions.question: How does a decision tree choose between candidate splits?
options: It picks the split that sends the most rows down a single branch
It picks the split on the feature that has the largest numeric values
It picks the split whose child nodes are purest, for example the lowest weighted Gini
It picks the split that keeps the child nodes as mixed as possible to avoid bias
questions.explanation: Splitting is a search for the cut that makes the resulting groups as pure as possible.

questions.question: A tree grown until every leaf holds a single training row scores 100% on training data and 70% on test data. What is the best fix?
options: Grow it deeper so the remaining test errors are also memorized
Standardize the features so that the splits become less extreme
Remove the test set so the gap can no longer be measured
Cap the maximum depth or require a minimum number of rows per leaf
questions.explanation: Limiting depth or leaf size (or pruning) stops the tree memorizing rows.

questions.question: Which statement about preparing features for a decision tree is true?
options: Scaling is not required, because each split compares one feature with a threshold
Scaling is required, because splits add up the values of several features at once
Standardizing is required, because splits assume the features are normally distributed
Scaling is required, because trees measure the distance between whole rows
questions.explanation: A threshold on one feature is unaffected by the scale of the others, unlike a distance-based method such as KNN.

questions.question: What is information gain?
options: The count of extra rows that a split sends to the larger child node
The drop in entropy from a parent to its children, weighted by size
The rise in the tree's depth after a new split has been added to it
The average entropy of the leaves after the whole tree is grown
questions.explanation: The split with the largest information gain makes the biggest step toward purity.

questions.question: Why can a decision tree change a lot when a few training rows change?
options: Trees store every training row, so deleting any row removes one of the leaves
Trees re-estimate their weights after each update, so small changes pile up
Each split is chosen greedily, so one new early split reshapes what follows
Trees depend on the row order, so shuffling the rows always rebuilds them
questions.explanation: This instability is a reason to use ensembles such as random forests.

questions.question: A decision tree can only be used when the target is a category.
questions.explanation: Regression trees predict a number, typically the average target in a leaf.

questions.question: In a two-class problem, a node with Gini impurity 0.5 is as mixed as it can be.
questions.explanation: 0.5 is the maximum Gini impurity for two classes.

questions.question: The first test at the top of a decision tree is called the ____ node. (one word)
questions.explanation: The root is the starting question.

questions.question: Match each decision tree term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The first test, at the top of the tree
A test on one feature that routes rows to branches
Holds the final prediction
Cutting branches back to reduce overfitting

questions.question: Describe how a decision tree decides where to split, using Gini impurity or entropy, and explain one way to keep a tree from overfitting.
questions.modelAnswer: At each node the tree tries candidate splits on the features and picks the one whose child nodes are purest, meaning lowest weighted Gini impurity or the highest information gain (biggest drop in entropy). A pure node has Gini 0 and entropy 0. It repeats on each child until the leaves are pure or a limit is reached. A fully grown tree memorizes the training data, so overfitting is limited by capping max_depth, requiring a minimum number of rows per leaf, or pruning branches.
rubric: Says the tree picks the split that makes the child nodes purest
Names Gini impurity or entropy (or information gain) as the measure
Notes that a pure node scores 0
Gives a way to limit overfitting: depth limit, minimum leaf size or pruning

questions.question: A single deep tree overfits. What does a random forest change to reduce this?
options: It grows one tree wider so that every leaf can hold more rows at once
It trains one tree on all rows and removes only its least used branches
It trains each tree on identical rows and features with different depth limits
It averages many trees that each saw different rows and features, so their errors differ
questions.explanation: Different trees make different mistakes, and combining them cancels many out. That lowers variance.

questions.question: What is a bootstrap sample?
options: Rows drawn with replacement, so some repeat and others are left out
Rows drawn without replacement, so each row appears at most once
A copy of the data in which every feature has been standardized or rescaled
The rows held out for the final test and never used in training
questions.explanation: Drawing with replacement gives each tree a slightly different version of the training data.

questions.question: Why does each split in a random forest consider only a random subset of the features?
options: So the forest never needs to scale the features before splitting them
So the trees differ from one another and do not all make the same mistakes
So each tree can concentrate on the single most important feature
So the trees can be trained without any bootstrap sampling of rows
questions.explanation: If every tree could use the strongest feature, all the trees would look alike and averaging would help less.

questions.question: How does a random forest classifier produce its final prediction?
options: The deepest tree's prediction is used, since it saw the most detail
The first tree's prediction is used and the rest only double-check it
Each tree votes and the class with the most votes wins
The tree with the lowest training error is used on its own
questions.explanation: The forest combines all its trees by majority vote.

questions.question: How does a random forest regressor predict a number?
options: It takes the most common prediction among its trees
It uses the largest prediction among all its trees
It fits a straight line through the trees' predictions
It averages the predictions of all its trees
questions.explanation: Voting is for classification. Regression averages.

questions.question: What are out-of-bag rows?
options: Rows left out of a tree's bootstrap sample, usable to check that tree
Rows with missing values that a tree is unable to split on at all
Rows the forest labeled as outliers and then removed
Rows kept for the final test set and never trained on at all
questions.explanation: About one third of the rows are left out of each bootstrap sample, giving a free validation estimate.

questions.question: What happens when more trees are added to a random forest?
options: Each tree gets deeper, so overfitting rises steadily with every tree added
Results steady and overfitting stays low, but training and prediction take longer
Training time falls because the work is shared out across the trees
Accuracy on the training data always climbs until it finally reaches 100%
questions.explanation: More trees reduce randomness in the result at the cost of time and memory.

questions.question: Compared with one decision tree, a random forest is
options: Usually less accurate, but easier to read as a set of rules
Usually faster to train, and just as easy to read as a set of rules
Usually more accurate and stable, but harder to read as a set of rules
Usually more accurate, and easier to read because it averages away detail
questions.explanation: A forest trades readability and speed for accuracy and stability.

questions.question: Combining many models so that their joint prediction beats any single one is called
options: Cross-validation, which rotates which rows are held out
Regularization, which penalizes large coefficients
Dimensionality reduction, which builds fewer new features
Ensemble learning
questions.explanation: A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees.

questions.question: In a random forest, every tree is trained on exactly the same rows.
questions.explanation: Each tree gets its own bootstrap sample.

questions.question: Averaging the predictions of many trees lowers variance compared with relying on one deep tree.
questions.explanation: Averaging many different trees smooths out their individual errors.

questions.question: The rows drawn with replacement to train each tree in a random forest form a ____ sample. (one word)
questions.explanation: Bootstrap sampling is the 'bagging' part of a random forest.

questions.question: A single deep tree overfits, yet a forest of such trees often does not. Explain what the forest does differently that improves its results on new data.
questions.modelAnswer: A single deep tree overfits: it memorizes the training data and changes a lot if the data changes. A random forest trains many trees, each on a bootstrap sample (rows drawn with replacement) and with only a random subset of features considered at each split, so the trees are different from each other. Classification takes a majority vote and regression takes the average. Because the trees make different errors, many of the errors cancel, so the forest has lower variance and overfits less.
rubric: Says a single deep tree overfits or is unstable
Mentions bootstrap samples and/or random feature subsets that make the trees differ
Says predictions are combined by voting or averaging
Concludes that errors cancel, giving lower variance and better generalization

questions.question: A model predicts monthly rent from square_feet (coefficient 1.8) and distance_to_center (coefficient -35). What does -35 mean?
options: With square_feet held constant, each extra unit of distance lowers predicted rent by 35
Rent falls by exactly 35 for every extra unit of distance, whatever else changes
Distance explains 35% of the variation in rent across all the listings
The model's error shrinks by 35 each time the distance increases by one unit
questions.explanation: A coefficient is the change in the prediction per one-unit change in that feature, holding the others constant. It is an association, not proof of cause.

questions.question: In the model y = 12 + 3x1 + 2x2, what does the 12 represent?
options: The amount y rises for each extra feature added
The predicted y when both features equal 0
The average of y across all the training rows
The error that is left over after the model is fitted
questions.explanation: 12 is the intercept, the prediction when every feature is 0.

questions.question: Using y = 12 + 3x1 + 2x2, what is the prediction when x1 = 4 and x2 = 5?
Which is an assumption of linear regression?
options: The features are all measured on the same scale as the target
The target takes only a few distinct category values to predict
The features are uncorrelated with the target they are meant to predict
The residuals have roughly constant spread across all predictions
questions.explanation: Constant variance of the residuals (homoscedasticity) is one. The features must relate to the target, and no scaling is required.

questions.question: What is multicollinearity?
options: Two or more features that are strongly correlated with each other
Two or more features that are strongly correlated with the target
A target that depends on several features through a curved relationship
Residuals whose spread grows with the size of the prediction
questions.explanation: It is correlation among the features, not between features and the target.

questions.question: A regression includes both square_feet and square_meters of the same houses. What is the likely consequence?
options: The model cannot be fitted at all because the two features use different units
Their coefficients become unstable, though predictions may stay accurate
Predictions become far less accurate and the R-squared drops to zero
The residuals will no longer be centered on zero after fitting
questions.explanation: Two features carrying the same information are the extreme case of multicollinearity: the model cannot split the credit between them.

questions.question: Two features have a correlation of 0.97 with each other. What is a sensible response?
options: Keep both and multiply them to build a stronger single feature
Drop whichever one correlates most strongly with the target
Drop one of them, or combine them, before fitting the model
Standardize both so that their correlation falls below 0.5
questions.explanation: Keep one representative. Scaling does not change a correlation.

questions.question: A feature has a very high VIF (variance inflation factor). What does this indicate?
options: It is the most predictive feature of the target in the model
It has a large number of missing values that must be filled
Its residuals are not normally distributed around zero in the plot
It is largely predictable from the other features
questions.explanation: VIF flags multicollinearity. Values above roughly 5 to 10 are a worry.

questions.question: On the training data, what happens to R-squared when you add a useless random feature to a linear regression?
options: It stays the same or rises slightly, hence adjusted R-squared
It always falls, since the random feature adds only noise
It rises sharply, because every feature adds real information
It becomes negative, since the feature is unrelated to the target
questions.explanation: Extra features can never reduce training R-squared, so adjusted R-squared penalizes them.

questions.question: Model A has an MSE of 4.0 and model B has an MSE of 9.0 on the same test set. Which statement is true?
options: Model B explains more variance because its MSE is larger
Model A's predictions are closer to the actual values on average
Model A is overfit because its MSE is lower than B's
The models cannot be compared because MSE has no units
questions.explanation: Lower MSE means smaller squared errors on the same data.

questions.question: A logistic regression outputs 0.83 for an email, using a 0.5 threshold. What happens?
options: The email is 83% spam-like text, so it gets a score but no class
The email is assigned to the negative class, since 0.83 is far from 1.0 and so unconvincing
It is assigned to the positive class, such as spam, since 0.83 beats 0.5
The model predicts 0.83 as the target value, as regression would
questions.explanation: Logistic regression outputs a probability and a threshold turns it into a class.

questions.question: Multicollinearity is about features correlated with each other, not features correlated with the target.
questions.explanation: Correlation with the target is what you want. Correlation among the features causes the problem.

questions.question: Logistic regression is a regression algorithm used to predict continuous numbers.
questions.explanation: Despite the name it is a classifier that outputs a probability.

questions.question: In regression, the actual value minus the predicted value is called the ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Residuals should be centered on zero with no pattern.

questions.question: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The prediction when every feature is 0
The change in prediction per one-unit change in a feature, others held constant
The actual value minus the predicted value
A check for features predictable from the other features

questions.question: Explain multicollinearity in a multiple linear regression: what it is, how you can detect it, and one way to handle it.
questions.modelAnswer: Multicollinearity means two or more of the features are strongly correlated with each other, so they carry overlapping information. The model cannot tell which one deserves the credit, so the coefficients become unstable: they swing in size or change sign when a feature is added or removed, even though predictions may stay fine. It can be detected with a correlation matrix of the features or with VIF (values above roughly 5 to 10 are a concern). It can be handled by dropping or combining the redundant features, using PCA, or using regularization such as Ridge.
rubric: Defines it as features correlated with each other
Says coefficients become unstable or hard to interpret
Names a way to detect it, such as a correlation matrix or VIF
Names a remedy, such as dropping or combining features, PCA or regularization

questions.question: A retailer has purchase histories but no labels and wants to find natural customer groups. Which approach fits?
options: Classification, because each customer needs to be assigned a class
Regression, because purchases are numeric values that need predicting
Supervised learning, because the purchase histories act as the labels
Clustering, because no target exists and the goal is to find structure
questions.explanation: With no target column the task is unsupervised, and grouping similar rows is clustering.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an unsupervised task?
options: Predicting a customer's next purchase amount from past purchases
Grouping customers who have similar buying habits
Compressing 60 survey columns into a few summary columns
Finding products that are often bought together in one basket
questions.explanation: Predicting a known numeric outcome is supervised regression. The others look for structure without a target.

questions.question: Which result would a good clustering produce?
options: Points within a cluster are far apart, and the clusters sit close to one another
Points within a cluster are close together and the clusters are far from each other
Every cluster contains exactly the same number of points as every other
Each cluster matches one of the known target labels in the data
questions.explanation: Clusters should be tight and well separated. There are no known labels to match.

questions.question: A news article is 70% 'sports' and 30% 'politics' under a clustering method. Which kind of clustering is this?
options: Hard, because each article is placed in its closest cluster
Density-based, because the article was found in a crowded region
Soft (fuzzy), because membership is shared across clusters
Hierarchical, because the article was merged into a larger cluster
questions.explanation: Soft clustering gives a degree of membership in several clusters instead of one.

questions.question: K-Means, hierarchical clustering and DBSCAN are grouped, in that order, as
options: Density-based, centroid-based and connectivity-based
Connectivity-based, density-based and centroid-based
Centroid-based, density-based and connectivity-based
Centroid-based, connectivity-based and density-based
questions.explanation: K-Means uses centroids, hierarchical clustering links clusters by connectivity, DBSCAN uses density.

questions.question: Why is judging an unsupervised result harder than judging a supervised one?
options: There are no known correct labels to compare the output against
The algorithms refuse to produce any numeric scores for their results
The data is always too small to be evaluated in any meaningful way
The features are not allowed to be compared between two separate runs
questions.explanation: Measures such as inertia or the silhouette score exist, but there is no answer key.

questions.question: What is the aim of dimensionality reduction?
options: Group the rows into clusters so that each row receives a cluster label
Represent the data with fewer features, keeping as much information as possible
Increase the number of features so that the model has more to learn from
Remove rows that look like outliers so that the data is cleaner overall
questions.explanation: Fewer features means faster, simpler models. PCA is the standard example.

questions.question: Which task finds items that tend to occur together, such as products bought in the same basket?
options: Regression, which predicts a continuous number from the features
Classification, which assigns each row to a predefined category
Association, also called data association
Binarization, which turns a numeric column into two groups
questions.explanation: Association is an unsupervised task alongside clustering.

questions.question: Unsupervised learning needs a target column to learn from.
questions.explanation: Unsupervised learning works on data with no labels.

questions.question: Clustering and dimensionality reduction are both unsupervised.
questions.explanation: Neither needs a target. Classification and regression are the supervised tasks.

questions.question: Clustering is a form of ____ learning, because it needs no labels. (one word)
questions.explanation: No labels means unsupervised.

questions.question: Match each method to its family.

pairs.right: Centroid-based clustering
Connectivity-based (hierarchical) clustering
Density-based clustering
Dimensionality reduction

questions.question: In K-Means, what happens in the update step?
options: Each point moves to the position of the centroid it is nearest to
Each cluster with fewer than k points is deleted from the model entirely
Each centroid is replaced by the point farthest from all the others
Each centroid moves to the mean of the points now assigned to it
questions.explanation: Assign points, then recompute each centroid as the mean of its cluster, and repeat.

questions.question: When does K-Means stop iterating?
options: When the assignments no longer change between iterations
When every cluster contains the same number of points
When the inertia reaches exactly zero
When every point has been used as a centroid once
questions.explanation: Once no point changes cluster, the centroids stop moving and the algorithm has converged.

questions.question: What does inertia measure in K-Means?
options: The sum of the distances between every pair of centroids
The sum of squared distances from each point to its assigned centroid
The number of points that changed cluster in the last iteration
The largest distance from any centroid to its farthest point
questions.explanation: Lower inertia means tighter clusters.

questions.question: On an elbow plot, inertia is plotted against k. How is the best k read?
options: At the k with the lowest inertia, since lower is always better
At the k where inertia first rises above the previous value
At the bend where adding clusters stops reducing inertia by much
At the k with the highest inertia, since that shows the most spread
questions.explanation: The elbow marks diminishing returns.

questions.question: Why can't you simply choose the k with the lowest inertia?
options: Inertia is lowest at k = 1, which is always too few clusters
Inertia only counts clusters with more than two points, so a small k is penalized
Inertia is undefined for values of k above 10 in scikit-learn
Inertia keeps falling as k grows, reaching 0 when every point is its own cluster
questions.explanation: More centroids always sit closer to the points, so the minimum would always pick the largest k.

questions.question: Why is K-Means sensitive to outliers?
options: A centroid is a mean, so one extreme point can pull it away from its cluster's center
A centroid is a median, so extreme points flip which cluster is chosen first
Outliers form a cluster of their own automatically, which uses up one value of k
Outliers increase the number of iterations until the algorithm fails to converge
questions.explanation: Means move toward extreme values, which drags the centroid and the cluster boundary with it.

questions.question: K-Means is run twice on the same data from different random starting centroids. What can happen?
options: The final clusters are always identical, since it converges to a single answer
The final clusters can differ, so it is rerun several times and the lowest inertia kept
The value of k differs, since the number of clusters is found automatically
The data differs, since the points are re-sampled on each run
questions.explanation: K-Means can settle in a local optimum. scikit-learn's n_init reruns it and keeps the best result.

questions.question: Centroids sit at (0, 0) and (6, 6). A point at (2, 1) is assigned to which, and by what rule?
options: The (6, 6) centroid, because larger coordinates carry more weight
The (0, 0) centroid, because it was listed first among the centroids
The (0, 0) centroid, because it is nearer by Euclidean distance
Neither centroid, because the point lies between the two of them
questions.explanation: Distance to (0, 0) is sqrt(5), about 2.2; distance to (6, 6) is sqrt(41), about 6.4.

questions.question: Why should features be scaled before running K-Means?
options: Centroids cannot be calculated for features that have large values
Scaling chooses the number of clusters automatically from the data
Scaling guarantees that the algorithm converges in a single iteration
Distances drive the assignments, so a feature with large values would dominate
questions.explanation: Like KNN, K-Means is distance-based.

questions.question: The points (1, 2), (3, 4) and (5, 9) are assigned to one cluster. Where does its centroid move?
K-Means requires you to choose the number of clusters before running it.
questions.explanation: k is an input. Elbow plots help to choose it.

questions.question: Inertia always increases when k increases.
questions.explanation: It decreases, reaching 0 when k equals the number of points.

questions.question: The center of a K-Means cluster, found as the mean of its points, is called the ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Centroid-based clustering is named after it.

questions.question: Describe the steps of K-Means and explain how an elbow plot helps choose k.
questions.modelAnswer: Choose k and place k starting centroids (randomly, or with k-means++). Assign every point to its nearest centroid using Euclidean distance. Move each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it. Repeat the assign and update steps until the assignments stop changing. Inertia is the sum of squared distances from each point to its centroid. It always falls as k grows, so an elbow plot of inertia against k is used instead: choose the k at the bend, after which extra clusters reduce inertia only a little.
rubric: Describes initialization, then assigning points to the nearest centroid
Describes moving each centroid to the mean of its points and repeating until stable
Defines inertia as the sum of squared distances to the centroids
Says the best k is at the elbow, where the drop in inertia levels off

questions.question: What does agglomerative clustering do at its first step?
options: Treats all points as one cluster, then splits off the farthest point
Treats every point as its own cluster, then merges the closest two
Places k centroids at random, then assigns each point to the nearest
Marks dense regions as cores, then expands outward from them
questions.explanation: Agglomerative is bottom-up: it starts with n clusters and merges. The other options describe divisive, K-Means and DBSCAN.

questions.question: On a dendrogram, what does the height at which two branches join represent?
options: The number of points inside the two clusters combined
The order in which the points first appeared in the original dataset
The distance between the two clusters when they were merged
The density of points around the place where they join
questions.explanation: Higher joins are merges of clusters that were further apart.

questions.question: A horizontal cut across a dendrogram crosses 4 vertical lines. How many clusters does the cut produce?
options: 3: one fewer than the number of lines crossed
5: one more than the number of lines crossed
2: the cut splits the tree into two halves
4: each crossed line is one cluster
questions.explanation: Count the vertical lines the cut crosses.

questions.question: Where is a good place to cut a dendrogram?
options: Across a tall vertical stretch with no merges, where clusters are far apart
At the very bottom, where every point is its own cluster
Across many short lines packed together, where merges are frequent
At the root, where all the points are in one cluster
questions.explanation: A long gap before the next merge suggests natural, well-separated clusters.

questions.question: Single linkage measures the distance between two clusters as
options: The distance between their farthest pair of points
The distance between their closest pair of points
The average distance over all pairs of points
The distance between the two clusters' centroids
questions.explanation: Single = minimum, complete = maximum, average = mean over pairs.

questions.question: Which linkage uses the farthest pair of points and tends to give compact clusters?
options: Single linkage
Average linkage
Complete linkage
Divisive linkage
questions.explanation: Complete linkage is the maximum pairwise distance. Single linkage uses the minimum.

questions.question: Which linkage is most likely to produce long, stringy, chained clusters?
options: Complete linkage
Average linkage
Ward linkage
Single linkage
questions.explanation: One close pair is enough to merge two clusters, so chains of nearby points join up.

questions.question: What is an advantage of hierarchical clustering over K-Means?
options: You need not choose the number of clusters up front
It runs faster on datasets with millions of rows
It always produces round clusters of equal size
It undoes a merge if the merge later turns out to be poor
questions.explanation: The dendrogram shows every level, and you choose where to cut afterwards.

questions.question: Why is agglomerative clustering hard to use on very large datasets?
options: It requires every feature to be categorical before any merging can start
It uses all pairwise distances, which grow fast as points are added
It must be rerun once for every possible value of k
It cannot handle more than three features at a time during merging
questions.explanation: n points give about n squared / 2 distances.

questions.question: Points on a number line sit at 1, 2, 5 and 9. Which two does agglomerative clustering merge first?
options: 5 and 9, the pair that is farthest from the others
2 and 5, because 5 is the middle point of the set
1 and 2, the closest pair at distance 1
1 and 9, the pair spanning the whole range
questions.explanation: The first merge is always the two closest clusters.

questions.question: A merge made in agglomerative clustering can be undone later.
questions.explanation: Merges are permanent, which is one weakness of the method.

questions.question: Agglomerative clustering is a bottom-up approach.
questions.explanation: It starts with single points and merges upward.

questions.question: The tree diagram showing the order and distance of cluster merges is called a ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Cut it with a horizontal line to choose the clusters.

questions.question: Match each linkage to how it measures the distance between two clusters.

pairs.right: Closest pair of points
Farthest pair of points
Mean over all pairs of points
The merge that raises within-cluster variance the least

questions.question: In DBSCAN, raising eps while keeping min_samples fixed tends to
options: Split clusters apart and add noise, since each neighborhood contains fewer points
Increase the number of clusters, since every point seeks out its own
Make no difference, since only min_samples decides which points are core
Merge clusters and reduce noise, since each neighborhood contains more points
questions.explanation: A bigger radius reaches more neighbors, so more points become core and clusters join.

questions.question: Raising min_samples while keeping eps fixed makes DBSCAN
options: Stricter about what counts as dense, so more points become noise
Looser about what counts as dense, so fewer points become noise
Faster to converge, while giving the same clusters as before
Return exactly min_samples clusters from the dataset
questions.explanation: Fewer points reach the higher neighbor count needed to be core.

questions.question: A point has only 2 neighbors inside eps (min_samples = 5) but sits within eps of a core point. What is it?
options: A core point: any point that lies within eps of another core point
A border point: part of a cluster but not dense enough to be core itself
A noise point: any point with fewer than min_samples neighbors
A centroid: it will be moved to the mean of the cluster
questions.explanation: Border points join a cluster through a nearby core point. Only points reachable from no core point are noise.

questions.question: What label does scikit-learn's DBSCAN give to noise points?
options: 0: the first cluster, as a default
The label of the nearest cluster, flagged as low confidence
-1: they belong to no cluster
NaN: the row is removed from the results
questions.explanation: Noise is labeled -1 and stays in the output.

questions.question: Which situation is a clear advantage of DBSCAN?
options: It always finds exactly the number of clusters you ask it to find
It works best when every cluster has a different density
It needs no distance measure, so features need no scaling
It finds crescent or ring shaped clusters and flags outliers as noise
questions.explanation: DBSCAN follows dense regions of any shape and does not force outliers into clusters.

questions.question: Which data would DBSCAN struggle with?
options: Clusters with very different densities, because one eps cannot suit them all
Clusters shaped like crescents, because only round blobs have core points
A dataset with a few outliers, because they must be assigned to a cluster
A dataset with no labels, because DBSCAN needs a target to learn from
questions.explanation: A single eps and min_samples define 'dense' for the whole dataset.

questions.question: How does DBSCAN decide how many clusters there are?
options: You supply k up front, as you do with K-Means
Each connected dense region becomes a cluster
A dendrogram is cut at a chosen height to select that count
The elbow of an inertia plot is read to select that count
questions.explanation: The count is a result of eps, min_samples and the data.

questions.question: A k-distance plot is used with DBSCAN to help choose which setting?
options: k, the number of clusters to find
The learning rate of the algorithm
eps, the neighborhood radius
The number of principal components to keep
questions.explanation: The bend in the sorted distances to each point's k-th neighbor suggests a good eps.

questions.question: What makes a point a core point in DBSCAN?
options: It sits at the exact mean position of its cluster
It is the point farthest from every noise point
It has the most neighbors of any point in the dataset
At least min_samples points lie within eps of it
questions.explanation: Core points are the dense ones from which clusters grow.

questions.question: DBSCAN requires you to specify the number of clusters in advance.
questions.explanation: You set eps and min_samples instead.

questions.question: In DBSCAN, a point can be left out of every cluster.
questions.explanation: Such points are labeled as noise.

questions.question: DBSCAN's two settings are eps and ____. (use the setting's name)
questions.explanation: min_samples is the neighbor count a point needs to be core.

questions.question: Match each DBSCAN term to its meaning.

pairs.right: The radius of the neighborhood around a point
Has at least min_samples neighbors within eps
Within eps of a core point but not core itself
Reachable from no core point and left unassigned

questions.question: A dataset with 30 features is reduced to 4 principal components. Which statement is correct?
options: The 4 columns are new features, each blending all 30 originals
The 4 columns are the original features that survived after 26 were dropped as noise
The 4 columns are cluster labels, one for each of four groups found in the data
The 4 columns are averages of the 30 features taken over each group of rows
questions.explanation: Principal components are weighted combinations of every original feature, not a subset of them.

questions.question: Five components explain 50%, 20%, 15%, 10% and 5% of the variance. What is the fewest components that keep at least 90%?
questions.explanation: Running totals: 50, 70, 85, 95. Three give only 85%, so four are needed.

questions.question: Why should features be standardized before PCA?
options: PCA cannot read features that have a mean above zero
PCA selects features by their correlation with the target, which scaling reveals
PCA chases variance, so a feature measured in large units would dominate
Standardizing turns the components back into the original features
questions.explanation: Without scaling, the component directions just follow the feature with the biggest numbers.

questions.question: Is PCA supervised or unsupervised, and why?
options: Supervised: it keeps the directions that best predict the target
Supervised: it needs labeled rows to find the components
Unsupervised: it groups the rows into clusters of similar rows
Unsupervised: it uses only the features and never looks at the target
questions.explanation: PCA works on the features alone. It reduces dimensions; it does not form clusters.

questions.question: Which direction does the first principal component follow?
options: The direction in which the data varies the most
The direction in which the data varies the least
The direction of the original feature with the largest mean
The direction that best separates the known classes
questions.explanation: Component 1 captures the greatest variance. Separating known classes is the job of LDA, a supervised method.

questions.question: How does PCA differ from LDA (linear discriminant analysis)?
options: PCA is supervised and maximizes class separation, while LDA is unsupervised and maximizes variance
PCA is unsupervised and maximizes variance, while LDA uses the labels to maximize class separation
Both are unsupervised, but LDA keeps every component while PCA keeps only a few
PCA selects original features, while LDA builds new features from the labels
questions.explanation: Both reduce dimensions, but only LDA uses the target.

questions.question: How are principal components related to one another?
options: They are identical copies, ordered by how many rows each one uses
They are nested, so each contains all of the earlier components
They are uncorrelated: each is perpendicular to the earlier ones
They are correlated by design so the variance is shared out evenly
questions.explanation: Each later component captures the most remaining variance at a right angle to those before it.

questions.question: Which is a typical application of PCA?
options: Predicting a numeric target from several features
Labeling emails as spam or not spam for a mail filter
Filling missing values with the column median
Reducing 50 features to 2 so the data can be plotted
questions.explanation: Visualization, speed-ups and noise reduction are the classic uses.

questions.question: What is the main cost of replacing features with principal components?
options: Each component blends all the features, so it is harder to interpret
The model can no longer be trained on numeric data afterwards
Rows must be removed so that the columns can be combined into new ones
The target column has to be dropped as well
questions.explanation: Any meaning has to be inferred from which features carry large weights in a component.

questions.question: On a scree plot of explained variance, where do you typically stop adding components?
options: Where the curve peaks, so each component adds the most
Where the curve flattens, so extra components add little variance
At the first component, since it holds all of the information
Where the curve crosses zero, since negative variance is noise
questions.explanation: A scree plot shows diminishing returns, like an elbow plot.

questions.question: PCA ignores the target variable.
questions.explanation: It is unsupervised: it only looks at the features.

questions.question: The explained variance ratios of all the components together add up to 100%.
questions.explanation: Together the components hold all the variance. Keeping fewer keeps a share of it.

questions.question: The new features that PCA creates are called principal ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Principal components.

questions.question: Explain what PCA does, how you choose the number of components to keep, and one drawback of using it.
questions.modelAnswer: PCA builds a smaller set of new, uncorrelated features called principal components, each a weighted combination of all the original features. The first captures the most variance and each later one the most of what remains. It is unsupervised and works best after standardizing. To choose how many to keep, add up the explained variance ratios (or read a scree plot) and keep enough components to reach a target such as 90 to 95%. A drawback is that components are blends of the original features, so they are hard to interpret, and the variance in the dropped components is lost.
rubric: Says PCA builds new uncorrelated features (components) from combinations of the originals
Says components are ordered by the variance they capture
Explains choosing components by cumulative explained variance or a scree plot
Gives a drawback, such as lost interpretability or lost variance

questions.question: What does a single perceptron compute?
options: The average of its inputs, passed through the loss function
The distance from its inputs to the nearest centroid, passed through a threshold
A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function
The product of its inputs and a bias, passed through backpropagation
questions.explanation: output = activation(w1x1 + w2x2 + ... + b).

questions.question: During training, a weight is pushed toward zero. What does that mean for its input?
options: The input is being treated as the most important one
The input is being removed from the dataset's table
The input's activation function has been changed to ReLU
The input has less and less influence on the neuron's output
questions.explanation: A weight scales the signal on its connection. Near 0 it contributes almost nothing.

questions.question: In a neuron computing sigmoid(w*x + b), what does the bias b do?
options: It shifts the point at which the neuron switches on
It scales how strongly x affects the output
It records how often the network has been wrong so far in training
It pulls the output toward the majority class
questions.explanation: The bias is a learned constant added to the weighted sum.

questions.question: Which of these is a hyperparameter, not a learned parameter?
options: A bias value in a hidden neuron
The number of hidden layers, chosen before training
A weight on a connection between two layers
The gradient computed for a weight at the last step
questions.explanation: Weights and biases are learned. The architecture and learning rate are set by the designer.

questions.question: A network with five layers uses only linear activations. What can it learn?
options: More than a single linear model, since each layer adds complexity
Simple patterns in the first layer and curves in the later layers
Only what one linear model could learn, since the layers collapse into one
Nothing, since linear activations stop the weights from updating
questions.explanation: Stacked linear transformations are still one linear transformation. Non-linear activations give depth its power.

questions.question: What does the ReLU activation output for inputs of -3 and 4?
options: -3 and 4
0 and 1
3 and 4
0 and 4
questions.explanation: ReLU(x) = max(0, x).

questions.question: Which activation function has outputs that range from -1 to 1?
options: Tanh
Sigmoid
ReLU
Softmax
questions.explanation: Sigmoid is 0 to 1, ReLU is 0 and above, and softmax gives probabilities that sum to 1.

questions.question: A network must pick among 6 classes. What does its output layer typically use?
options: One neuron with ReLU, whose value is rounded to a class number
Six neurons with softmax, so the outputs are probabilities that sum to 1
Six neurons with step functions, so every output is 0 or 1
One neuron with sigmoid, whose value is split into six equal ranges
questions.explanation: Multiclass output uses one neuron per class with softmax.

questions.question: A network has 8 input features, two hidden layers, and predicts one number. How many neurons does its input layer have?
options: 1, one per target value
2, one per hidden layer
8, one per feature
16, one per feature in each hidden layer
questions.explanation: The input layer has one neuron for each feature.

questions.question: A dense layer takes 6 inputs and has 4 neurons. How many weights and biases does it have in total?
questions.explanation: Weights: 6 x 4 = 24. Biases: 4, one per neuron. Total 28.

questions.question: According to the course, a network counts as deep learning when it has
options: Two or more hidden layers between the input and output
More than ten hidden layers between input and output
A hidden layer and an output layer of its own
Any activation function other than a step function
questions.explanation: Deep learning uses neural nets with 2+ hidden layers.

questions.question: What is a downside of making a network much larger, with many more layers and neurons?
options: It loses the ability to represent curved boundaries
It can overfit the data and costs much more to train
It can no longer be trained with gradient descent at that size
It must use a step activation to stay stable
questions.explanation: More capacity can represent more complex patterns, but also memorize noise.

questions.question: Why can a single perceptron not learn XOR?
options: XOR has too many input features for one perceptron to read
A perceptron's activation cannot output both 0 and 1
The XOR classes cannot be separated by one straight line
XOR needs a loss function that perceptrons do not have
questions.explanation: A perceptron draws a single linear boundary. Hidden layers with non-linear activations solve XOR.

questions.question: A neural network's weights are set by hand and stay fixed during training.
questions.explanation: Weights and biases are the values that change during training.

questions.question: A network that predicts a house price typically has a single neuron in its output layer.
questions.explanation: One number to predict means one output neuron.

questions.question: The learned constant added to a neuron's weighted sum is called the ____. (one word)
questions.explanation: Weights and biases together are the network's parameters.

questions.question: Match each neural network term to its role.

pairs.right: Scales how much one input influences a neuron
Shifts the point at which a neuron activates
Adds non-linearity to a neuron's output
Sits between the input layer and the output layer

questions.question: In gradient descent, what is the gradient of the loss with respect to a weight?
options: The size of the next step taken, regardless of what the loss is
The value the weight would have if training were finished
The share of training rows that the weight was updated on
How much the loss changes when that weight changes slightly
questions.explanation: The gradient points uphill. The update moves the weight the opposite way.

questions.question: With w = 5, a gradient of 2 and a learning rate of 0.1, what is the weight after one gradient descent step?
questions.explanation: w_new = 5 - 0.1 x 2 = 4.8. The step goes against the gradient.

questions.question: During training the loss jumps up and down and sometimes grows. What is the likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too small, so the steps never reach the minimum
The learning rate is too large, so the steps overshoot the minimum
The network has too few hidden layers to represent the pattern
The test set is too small to give a stable score
questions.explanation: Overshooting makes the loss bounce or blow up. A learning rate that is too small gives slow, steady progress instead.

questions.question: Training is very slow, with the loss falling by tiny amounts each epoch. What is the likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too large, so each step overshoots
The network has too many output neurons for the targets
The learning rate is too small, so each step is tiny
The activation function has been set to ReLU everywhere
questions.explanation: Tiny steps mean slow progress toward the minimum.

questions.question: What does backpropagation compute?
options: The new weights themselves, using the learning rate and the previous weights
The network's predictions, found by working forward from the inputs to the output
The best number of layers and neurons for the data it is given, by trial
The gradient of the loss for every weight and bias, found working backward
questions.explanation: Backpropagation applies the chain rule backward through the layers to get the gradients.

questions.question: How do backpropagation and gradient descent relate?
options: Backpropagation supplies the gradients and gradient descent uses them to update the weights
Gradient descent supplies the gradients and backpropagation uses them to update the weights
They are two names for the same single step of training
Backpropagation chooses the loss function and gradient descent chooses the activation
questions.explanation: Backpropagation finds the direction. Gradient descent takes the step.

questions.question: What is an epoch?
options: One update of a single weight in the network
One full pass of all the training data through the network
One layer of neurons in the network, input to output
One small batch of rows used in a single update
questions.explanation: A batch is the group of rows used per update. An epoch is a pass over all of them.

questions.question: What does the loss function do?
options: It decides which neurons are removed from the network
It sets the learning rate for each epoch
It scores how far the predictions are from the true targets
It splits the data into training and test sets
questions.explanation: Training tries to make the loss small. MSE and cross-entropy are common losses.

questions.question: A network updates its weights after each group of 32 training rows. Which variant is this?
options: Batch gradient descent, which uses every row for each update
Stochastic gradient descent, which uses one row for each update
Backpropagation through time, which is used for each epoch
Mini-batch gradient descent
questions.explanation: Mini-batch is the usual compromise between one row and all rows.

questions.question: Which order describes one training step?
options: Forward pass, compute the loss, backpropagate the gradients, update the weights
Compute the loss, forward pass, update the weights, backpropagate the gradients
Update the weights, forward pass, compute the loss, backpropagate the gradients
Backpropagate the gradients, update the weights, forward pass, compute the loss
questions.explanation: You need a prediction before a loss, a loss before gradients, and gradients before an update.

questions.question: Gradient descent finds the best weights by trying every possible combination of them.
questions.explanation: It takes many small steps downhill on the loss instead.

questions.question: Raising the learning rate always makes training converge faster.
questions.explanation: Too large a rate overshoots and can make the loss grow.

questions.question: The setting that scales each gradient descent update is called the ____ rate. (one word)
questions.explanation: Learning rate: new weight = old weight - learning rate x gradient.

questions.question: Describe one training iteration of a neural network, naming the forward pass, the loss, backpropagation and the gradient descent update.
questions.modelAnswer: In the forward pass the inputs flow through the layers (weights, biases and activations) to produce a prediction. The loss function, such as MSE or cross-entropy, scores how far the prediction is from the true target. Backpropagation then works backward from the output using the chain rule to find the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight and bias. Gradient descent updates each parameter against its gradient: new weight = old weight - learning rate x gradient. Repeating this over many epochs lowers the loss.
rubric: Describes the forward pass producing a prediction
Says a loss function measures the error
Says backpropagation computes the gradients backward through the layers
Gives the update w = w - learning rate x gradient
